C0.quote: present a unified framework for grading-based voting processes

C1.quote: satisfies the properties Neutrality, Universality, and Unanimity
C1.note: Main results are properties and characterisations of deepest voting rules, plus paradox analysis.

C2.1.quote: The grading is summarized in a d × n grading matrix

C2.2.quote: Approval voting is a voting process based on a binary
C2.2.note: Grades in [0,1], discrete or continuous; the binary case gives approval voting.

C2.3.quote: the deepest point is a location estimator of the preferences
C2.3.note: Preferences are also mentioned in the paradox discussion: 'voter v3 prefers candidate c2'.

C2.4.note: Doubt between DIST and IDU. Grades are described as submitted, but also as voters' preferences. The text on strategic and sincere voting says votes may differ from preferences, so DIST, the first-listed code, is chosen.

C3.1.quote: very vulnerable to strategic voting for a large p
C3.1.note: Strategic voting is mentioned only informally; no analysis models misreporting.

C3.2.note: Sincere voting appears only inside the no-show paradox definition. The paper never states as an assumption that voters submit their held attitudes.

C4.1.quote: they introduce the intensity of the relative preferences
C4.1.note: C2.2 includes APPR and the paper uses intensity of preference for voters, so the item applies. Grades are said to convey intensity, but no formal link to utilities is defined.

C5.1.note: Results concern neutrality, universality, unanimity, monotonicity, IIA and Condorcet/no-show/reinforcement paradoxes; none of the listed criteria are used.

VOT.quote_behav: Suppose that each voter vj , j = 1, . . . , n grades
VOT.note: Voters act by grading candidates. The grades are taken as given, with no strategic choice modelled.

C8.1.note: NA: no agent type is strategic.

claims.quote: can be seen as the most representative of all voters
do not lead to monotone voting procedures, which seems a main drawback

C9.2.quote: their preferences should meet a large consensus among the others
C9.2.note: The representativeness/consensus claim needs grades to equal voters' held preferences; this is not stated as an assumption.

C2.4.reason: The paper's references to strategic versus sincere voting are text saying the submitted grades may differ from held preferences, which fits DIST at least as well as IDU, so the first-listed code applies.

C3.2.reason: The phrase 'vote sincerely' only defines a paradox and is not a statement that voters in the analyses submit their held attitudes.

C3.3.reason: C3.3 is NA because C3.2 is NOT-STATED.

C4.1.reason: The applicability condition holds (APPR input plus 'intensity of preference'), and the relation is only mentioned, not defined.

C6.VOT.reason: Voters take an action in the model (grading candidates) that is fixed exogenously, so they are present and NONSTRAT.
